utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you allow me to respond, I would say good afternoon, Mr. Registrar, but it's good that you're still morning fresh. There are two minor matters which I would just like to raise for a second. We asked Mr. Krajisnik -- I think it was last Friday but I'm not sure about that, to read the first two lines on what was his page 0322-1 -- 0531. Yes. The transcript now reflects exactly what I said, but that might create some confusion. So I repeat the number: 0322-0531. Yes. Since there was a problem with the translation, the Chamber asked the CLSS to verify the translation of this document on which this page appears, and then specifically on these two lines. CLSS has, however, a problem there because the original translation is not theirs. It seems to be an OTP-produced translation. Therefore, they suggested to have the whole of the document freshly translated, which might take considerable time. I tend to invite CLSS to translate specifically, so not commenting on the existing translation, but to freshly translate the two lines and invite the Defence to identify any further translation issue that might appear in this document, because to have seven pages translated since we found -- we identified one translation problem in two lines, it takes a lot of resources. Therefore I would first prefer to have verification, whether the remainder of the translation causes any real problem, that is any problem apart from some variety in language that could always be there but whether it would be prejudicial to the Defence. Perhaps if Mr. Sladojevic could perhaps have a look at it. But before doing so, I'd like to see whether there is any submission to be made in this respect from the parties as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we consider that Your Honour's suggestion is far and away the most sensible way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that saves us six pages and approximately 35 lines to be translated. Then we'll do it this way. Mr. Registrar, you -- would you please present to CLSS the two lines and one line prior to that, one line after that, to be retranslated freshly and then we, I take it that we hear within a week from the Defence if there is any further need to have the remainder of the document to be translated. That's one issue. Then there is a second issue I would like to briefly raise. I was informed, Mr. Krajisnik, that a floppy disk which comes from you went, I don't know for what reasons, went to the OTP, is now sent back to the Defence and there was a personal matter on it and therefore you would like to receive it back from the Defence. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just take a minute of your time? During my arrest, the SFOR took certain documentation from me, including one floppy disk, the graduation paper of my son, and at the request of the Defence team, the OTP returned that floppy disk to my Defence team. I am unable to contact them right now and they have still not found a way to give me that file, nor are they able to open it. So I am sort of left without a choice and I have to request your assistance in having that returned to me. Maybe you can take a few minutes to find out what it is about and I'm sure the Office of the Prosecutor knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I know about this, Your Honour, at least I know what Mr. Krajisnik is talking about. Shortly before he gave evidence, the Prosecution disclosed various arrest documents, or documents relating to Mr. Krajisnik's arrest, to us. That included an old-fashioned floppy disk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The big one, the real floppy one, or is it a 3 and a half inch?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Small but not one that's capable of going into a CD reader. And frankly we were unable to open it. The extent to which we made efforts to open it I can't tell the Court. At some juncture I had made an arrangement with Mr. Krajisnik that he would open it in my presence. Due to an oversight on my part, that proved impossible; frankly I forgot it at the relevant meeting. He thought he would be able to open it on the equipment he had available to him at the detention unit. So that hasn't happened. We are still in possession of it; it's actually in this building. Probably we should open it first of all, but I suspect Mr. Harmon knows what's in it, not now, I appreciate he doesn't know now, but I suspect someone in the OTP will know what's on it. Perhaps I could speak to them at the next break and we could then revert to this subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Opening you mean to open by what programme so the file doesn't open and is not visible on your screen? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right. We've been unable to physically open it in that sense, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do I understand that you -- you identified on that floppy disk which document it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. But Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He knows?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He inferred that it must be a particular file, which he said to me, I'm sure he won't mind me saying this, included work done by his son six years ago when he was arrested. Whether that's right, we can't say until it's been opened but that is what Mr. Krajisnik thought was on the disk. Whether there is anything else on the disk, I have no idea, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been returned to the Defence. I'm looking to you, Mr. Harmon. Is there any hesitation to just return the floppy disk to Mr. Krajisnik? Because I do understand that if it's returned to the Defence that the Prosecution would have no problem in -- and it is -- has the same content as six years ago, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I take it does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because it has been in your hands for all this time. Would, under those circumstances, would there be any major problem just to return the floppy disk Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: None at all. That could be done this afternoon, I'm pretty sure, I'm fairly confident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has no difficulties that you would return the floppy disk, of course, within all the security settings as defined by the Registrar to return it to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If Mr. Krajisnik feels there is anything on the disk which is important to his evidence, then I would invite him to bring that to our attention in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, of course, first seek leave from the Bench --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to further discuss the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That was assumed in the remark I just made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just remind Mr. Krajisnik of this rule. So therefore, both matters are resolved now. We'll now continue, but not until after I have reminded you, Mr. Krajisnik, as you know, I always do, all witnesses, that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart or Mr. Josse, whoever it is, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you have the bundle of intercepts that you were permitted to take with you to the detention unit this weekend? I see that you do.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We had got to number 3 on this mini list. I'd now like to turn to number 4, which is an intercept again between yourself and Mr. Karadzic, sometime in January of 1992. As far as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that one which has no exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As far as our records indicate that is the position so could I ask for a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D187, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't intend to play this, Mr. Krajisnik. At the beginning of the conversation, we see that you say --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a second, please. There are several intercepts from January. Which one of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said it was number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- fourth one in your bundle and --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we see at the top of the intercept that you say that you've been called by Vojo Kupresanin. You go on and say it would be good if someone went there, but swearing it would be good if someone could now, you know, explain this about the finances, they want the whole Krajina, stop paying tomorrow. What's this about, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I read this intercept, I wrote a note that reads, "I don't know what this is about." However, having thought about it and analysed it a bit, I can now recall that in January at one point, the Autonomous Region of Krajina wished on its own initiative to stop its contributions and payments towards the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, into the budget of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And there is reference here to the opinion that that shouldn't be done unilaterally and there is a reference to the conversation between me, Mr. Karadzic, and the president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Mr. Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So what was your view on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever we were talking finance, the position was always that we should decentralise the budget and that the existing centralisation, the one in Sarajevo, should be decentralised as much as possible and funds returned to the regions. But this specific conversation was about a unilateral decision and we were against doing it that way. We wanted instead to reach a solution through negotiations, and there were some negotiations in January, and we thought it was possible because the Muslims and Croats were also in favour of that solution, and we were about to finalise this deal. This concerned funds for health care, old age pensions, et cetera, and all the other funds that were regulated and collected at the level of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what was your concern as to what might happen to the ARK finances if they took this course? To put it another way did you fear there might be some retaliation from the republic government?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was at stake were economic interests. As in every state, the centre, Sarajevo, was a large economic centre, and when revenues are high, contributions are also high, and we were saying -- we were discussing in this conversation whether it would -- whether it pays off to make contributions, to continue making contributions, whether what they received offsets their contributions or they should withdraw their contributions subject to a tripartite consent because any unilateral position and we who defended Serb interests knew this perfectly well, would damage the negotiating positions of the Serbs because the other side would tell us, "You are doing something that we hadn't agreed about," whereas we always kept saying, "We are reacting to your unilateral moves because you started violating our earlier agreements."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like now, please, to turn to the next intercept in the bundle. Same two protagonists. This was sometime in February of 1992. It has been exhibited as part of 64 A and 154.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand it's never been played. Again I don't intend to play it now. I'm not in fact sure whether it's been referred to previously in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we turn in the English to the second page, please, and at the top of the page. I'll read it slowly, Mr. Krajisnik, whilst the place is found. You say, "I had to give them a boost, not to make silly moves like Brdjanin and Kupresanin and then I first did that and then I made an agreement for them to translate that and thirdly the constitutional committee to prepare it. Alija called me." "Yes," says Karadzic. You say, "Is it true that you're going to proclaim the constitution on Friday? It is confusing. You didn't tell him Friday but tomorrow." What are you saying there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two issues are discussed here. I'll start with the second one. When he asks me, "Did you convene the proclamation of the constitution for Friday? Did you schedule it for Friday?", I, in reply, convey the discussion I had with Mr. Izetbegovic and I tell him that it's scheduled for the next day, the 26th, on the 25th February, I don't know when this conversation took place. Whereas this first passage, where Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Kupresanin are mentioned is something else. We were following the unconstitutional moves plead by the other sides and we reacted to them. However, there was great concern in the Krajina and especially on the part of Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Kupresanin, who kept saying that we, our side, is constantly making some moves which are dictated in a way by the other side, whereas they are following their ambition to create an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina at an accelerated tempo. We agreed to a transformation along the lines of decentralisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina but not to a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina. You saw our draft constitution that we made where we specified that this constitution that we were about to adopt was going to be an integral part of the outcome of negotiations on Bosnia-Herzegovina. So our policy was to keep the negotiations going, to keep this as a link, whereas the people from Krajina thought that ours was an exercise in futility, that they were following their objective of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina along a different track and unfortunately they turned out to be right later because they got their independence and we did not get the transformation as agreed. However at this point I was trying to persuade them to refrain from unilateral moves and I was trying to boost their morale and appease their concerns. When I read this through I recalled that time. It came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I make an observation about the next document? This is part of P154, though I don't have it in front of me, I think on the exhibit list this still appears as being under seal. It shouldn't be. I've had some correspondence with Mr. Zahar on the subject and he confirmed that it should not be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we check that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I followed that correspondence as well. That's consistent with my understanding, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not in my recollection any more but having been informed that P154 is one of the documents tendered through the late Mr. Babic, I think we gave a -- kind of a general order on that so that would then be public and it should be indicated on the list that it is a public document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I could assist, that's from 152 through to 156 inclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You may proceed in public session now with 154 and we'll verify where things went wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, again, according to our researches, the intercept that I'm about to refer to has never been alluded to in any way at all in court. It's simply part of the Babic intercept collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I want to take you to the bottom of the first page in the English. This is a conversation again between you and Mr. Karadzic sometime in February of 1992. And Karadzic says, "I see they've removed Babic there." Krajisnik: "Well, I must tell you that they did the right thing." Karadzic: "Did the right thing, huh?" Krajisnik: "He can go fuck himself." Karadzic: "Right. One man who insists he can go fuck himself." Krajisnik: "There is no fucking way. I don't know what I would do. For a long timing I thought about whether we made a mistake but you have to be a rational Serb." Karadzic: "No. It's unbelievable that he values himself so much and he thinks he's more important than everything else. But he has to stand before the assembly and say to the people that we have a situation which is so" -- I'm afraid in the English it's not clear what that is. I think I'll ask you to read that in a moment back, and you decide and I'll do what you say. Could you read, Mr. Krajisnik, that answer from Mr. Karadzic into the record and so it can be translated again?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Well, no, it's incredible that he sees himself that way and he believes himself to be more important than anything. He has to come out before the assembly so that P ... and say, people, we have a situation here. And the situation is such and such. And I will do as you decide."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. And your response to that was, "Right."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you are interested with these dots, it was supposed to be "people." It was simply swallowed and the speech is a bit incoherent, but it's clear what Mr. Karadzic was saying. He is overestimating himself. What he should do is to come out in front of the assembly, explain the situation to them, and let them decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why are you and Mr. Karadzic happy that Mr. Babic has been removed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that we were happy. You can even see from my answer that we weren't. But we did support that move. If I may, I would like to remind Their Honours, when I was examined by Mr. Stewart about the meeting in Belgrade at which the Vance plan was supposed to be adopted, the entire meeting was ready to accept the plan and only Mr. Babic, late Mr. Babic, and his government, were against it. And the next day, when we were supposed to resume, he simply didn't show up. And an entire group of participants not from Republika Srpska went to attend an assembly meeting of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, to Glina, I believe, to replace Mr. Babic. Regarding the Vance plan, we were saying in this conversation that he needed to be rational, and I even questioned my own judgement, whether I was right, whether we were right, when we gave unreserved support to the Republic of Serbian Krajina, although not personally to Babic, and this ties in with the discussion that followed at the meeting of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next interpret, please. This is a conversation between you and Mr. Koljevic held sometime in February of 1992, part of P389. Again, I don't think it's ever been played or perhaps referred to. A few lines down, after the introductions, Mr. Koljevic says, "Horrible. I'd been in a real Ustasha nest in Slavonski Brod. Not even Tudjman controls it." What's that a reference to, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a conflict in Bosanski Brod, that is to say on the Bosnian side. The other side is Slavonski Brod. And a delegation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which included Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Ejub Ganic, they arrived in Bosanski Brod and established contact with Slavonski Brod which is across the Sava River. Because traffic had been stopped, interrupted, between Bosanski Brod and Slavonski Brod. And now, Mr. Koljevic here says that he saw various units over there that weren't even being controlled by the centre from Zagreb, and he had in mind the late Tudjman, and he's looking at it from his point of view and he said I was in a real Ustasha nest and what he had in mind was probably the people that had this insignia and reminded him of World War II. So he says here that they attacked Ejub Ganic and Bosnian politics, that they attacked him to a lesser extent, but that that was the reason for the conflict, and which had a negative repercussion later on, if you remember the Sijepovac [phoen] case where Mrs. Plavsic went and somebody -- somebody else to represent the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was a delegation. And Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Ganic were there in the name of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Presidency before the war, not on the part of the Muslim side or representing the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A few lines further on, you say, "Do you see, they went to the council and I have to go to a meeting up, then I'll go to the one down in what's its name, I have in Rajlovac some meeting in connection with this one municipality." Before I ask you a question about that, Mr. Krajisnik, could we look at the next intercept in the bundle, please, which has two numbers, it's also part of P389 but it's also P1135, would be relatively fresh in all of our memories because my learned friends for the Prosecution cross-examined Mr. Krsman about this particular intercept. It's a conversation again in February of 1992 between yourself and Mr. Karadzic. And near the top of the page, you say, "He's not -- he's gone down to Reljevo, so down there people, I'm right, is an idea, I have one, big territory, they want to establish Rajlovac municipality as it used to be, you know. You go on and say that's a big territory so then people want you to sit down with them, I stayed until late last night and I had to go to the constitutional commission so I asked Milos to go. I can't, that's Milos Savic." So there are two references to Rajlovac, one in the conversation with Mr. Koljevic, the other in the reference to Mr. Karadzic. Do they have anything in common and what are they about, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be a good idea if the interpreters had the original because I'm looking at the original and they are doing their best, but the sense here is quite different when it goes from Serbian into English and back from English into Serbian. So it would be a good idea if the interpreters had the original Serbian text and I'll tell you the mistake here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My observation on that, Your Honour, is this illustrates a problem which I came across in going through these with Mr. Krajisnik, is more than probably any other area of translation, these intercepts are particularly difficult to translate for obvious reasons. And this illustrates the point rather well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with you that it's not an easy task to do. At the same time we'll have to do our utmost best and I think it's certainly is of great value that these mistakes are now identified so that the Chamber will not be misled by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from having the original in front of the interpreters, Mr. Krajisnik, if there was a specific line you had in mind, you could perhaps slowly read that and see whether the -- and could you then please indicate to us exactly where you start reading so that the translation can be verified by the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the second conversation, I heard the interpreter say something different. I'll read it out and tell you what I heard. I'm just going to read out three lines and it's Krajisnik speaking, the M. 02079380 is the number. And it's Krajisnik speaking, the M: "So knackered you cannot imagine." "Ah," Radovan, that is, "so, resting or what?" He can't say "resting." He probably said, "You're resting." So he should have said, "Are you resting," not just "resting." Then, three, the third person is M again: "No. I had," where it says "he's not," and "he's gone," third person singular, whereas it should be "I," first person singular. And I'm going back to reading now. "No, I had -- went down there to Reljevo, and down there people -- I'm right." And then there is a question mark; "because there is an idea, there is a big territory, they want to establish a municipality, Rajlovac municipality, the kind that it used to be, you know." So here the problem is that I say, "I went to Reljevo and the people told me that they wished to establish a municipality." I'm not speaking about a third person. So it's not "he." And Karadzic asks me whether I'm resting, not "Is he resting, he's resting." He's asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for reading it again to us. If you just allow me a minute, I have not found it, but -- and I want to reread the -- what Mr. Krajisnik just read to us. We are in number 8, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are in number 8, correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then exactly on what page are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the English, we are in the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And obviously the same in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it just at the top, yes. I will now re-read what I see on the transcript at this moment. Yes. The question now is how to resolve it. Mr. Krajisnik, if you read the original, do you find that it's not transcribed properly? Is it a translation problem or is it a transcription problem? If it's a translation problem, then we would invite to have these couple of lines be translated anew and then invite the Defence to identify any other matter, any other translation problem they would find in this document. If, however, it is -- if the original is transcribed wrongly, then, of course, we should take different action. Could you tell us whether the -- we call it B/C/S and you call it Serbian -- whether that's properly transcribed, especially on the issues you just raised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from the fact that it's a little unwieldy, and hasn't been interpreted in a fluent way, perhaps it's like that in the original, but the sense in the original is not wrong. But when I listened to it, I don't know how it was interpreted into English, I didn't listen, but I was afraid that it might not be translated correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we'll then do is we'll do it on the same basis that we did it before, unless I hear any objection by the parties, that is that the first five boxes -- because that covers the problem, I would say, Mr. Josse, the first five boxes will be translated anew and that the Defence is invited to draw our attention to any other translation problem involved. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So Mr. Krajisnik, I showed you this passage and the one in the previous intercept, where there is a reference to you having a meeting in Rajlovac. First question is: Is this one and the same meeting being referred to or are they different meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same meeting. It's just that a broader concept of Rajlovac, if I can put it that way, was used, and a precise location, Reljevo, but that's a region. Rajlovac is a region, Reljevo is a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to be more specific as to when this meeting took place? When in February 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps if I think back and analyse the situation I might be able to tell you, but unfortunately off the cuff I can't. I didn't focus on that too much. But I do know that I did attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what was the meeting about and what was your role there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, you will recall that the president of the Novi Grad municipality testified here, Mr. Ismet Cengic, and he mentioned that there was an initiate on the part of people from Rajlovac to give the local community in June 1991, pursuant to standard procedure, or rather to give them a municipality and the municipal assembly discussed the situation. The local commune did not receive the go ahead and I talked to people privately and I always told Mr. Cengic at the time or rather I made him a promise that I would help them find a compromise solution, because it's my local commune, it's the village I lived in, and those deputies didn't do anything to make it possible to establish, following recommendations from the assembly, their own municipality, the Serbian municipality, and Rajlovac, after World War II, was indeed a municipality. And then I said that they had invited me to attend the meeting, in February, I was their deputy, I was from that place, myself, and then I expressed what their demands were. They wanted a municipality, and a referendum had already been called. It was common knowledge that things were not going through as they should be. So now we have a request from them to establish a municipality. And Mr. Cengic did read out some facts and figures, some information, and I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that had I had any knowledge about Variant A or B, it would have been presented to the people where I lived for them to be able to compile in January, December, and not in February when I went at their request to see what they actually wanted. And later on, the Rajlovac municipality was indeed established. It existed during the war. It was in existence throughout the war. So the meaning of this is that we called, that is to say deputies and citizens, called for this and the meeting was convened and everybody wanted to ask a question, and so I stayed there for a long time and discussed all this. It's just 500 metres from my house, Zabrdje Reljevo. I went to Reljevo to talk to Mr. Koljevic from Zabrdje, that is I went to Sarajevo where he had come to from Slavonski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the reference to Milos Savic going to the constitutional commission is what?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me a question but I've forgotten. Milos Savic was the deputy secretary of the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The deputy of Mr. Avdo Campara, on the Serb side. At one time he was president of the Novi Grad municipality. And I was supposed to go to the constitutional commission. Now, whether the constitutional commission of Republika Srpska or Bosnia-Herzegovina was supposed to convene, I don't know. I was a member of both. But I asked him to replace me, to take my place in that constitutional commission because I had to go to this other meeting where I'd been invited, the meeting in Reljevo. Mr. Milos Savic, he died since then, but he was the secretary of the Serbian assembly, later on, and throughout the war as well. You will recall the telephone conversation when I asked Mr. Mandic to release his family because his brother and sister-in-law from Bolje [phoen] Potok was supposed to be liberated and Mr. Mandic took it upon himself to see that that was done. So that's what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. The penultimate intercept of this bundle, please, which is one between yourself and Mrs. Karadzic initially, and then about halfway through the conversation Mr. Karadzic takes over. Also in February of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It needs a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conversation, Mrs. Karadzic says to you, "Not yet but Branko Simic from Capljina has just called. The Capljina garrison has been blocked since last night." What is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for asking me that. There was a misunderstanding here. Capljina is in Croatia n the Croatian part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and belongs to the Federation today. I'm sure the Presiding Judge will recall when I asked my lawyer a question and said that Capljina was in Croatia because a witness said that the Serbs had expelled Croats and (redacted) (redacted) was a mistake. He was wrongly informed by the media in Sarajevo. What this is about is that there was a garrison in Capljina, a garrison of the Yugoslav People's Army, and the HOS units -- first of all, they were extremist forces, Croatian extremist forces, they had blocked the Capljina garrison and later on the whole of Capljina was controlled by the HVO throughout the war. The Serbs had left the area. And for purposes of illustration, if I might just be allowed to digress, the son of a Presidency member was killed on the occasion of the Yugoslav state Presidency in that blockade. And now to get back to the question that counsel has just asked me, what happened, blockades started being set up around garrisons like they were in Croatia, and this began in the Croatian parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina first, and the reference to Branko Simic is this. He's the late Branko Simic. He was vice-president of the Serbian Assembly and he was a deputy of the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and he was the president of the commission for the control of National Defence, and he had come from Mostar where he lived. He phoned up Mrs. Karadzic to inform Mr. Karadzic that the garrison had been blocked in Capljina. So that is a useful piece of information for you to be able to see that this was a --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) It was the reverse. So this is by way of assistance to the Trial Chamber to be able to understand this in context. And there is some more important things here that I can say about Mr. Karadzic's visit, if you're interested in hearing it, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic's visit to what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a secret visit, in fact. Mr. Karadzic met with the Croatian side. I think it was in western Herzegovina because Mr. Karadzic had good relations, was on good terms, with the late Mr. Boban, who led the HDZ, and he had a meeting with him. He crossed from the Serb side to the Croatian side and had a meeting somewhere around Mostar, and when he refers to Branko Simic, who was a deputy, later on, he expressed his dissatisfaction as to why he did not know about this secret meeting, that someone should have informed him. It was a bilateral talk in order to find a solution to the situation, and mild pressure was brought to bear on the Muslim side to try and dovetail their agreements and not to refuse a compromise. I learned about this visit later on. I didn't know at the time. I didn't know when Mr. Karadzic actually went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to move on with the intercept, please. Just over the page in the English, you're still talking to Mrs. Karadzic, she has in fact indicated that her husband is returning home at that moment. You say, "You know what Cengic said today. Cengic said it was very interesting. Cengic said" -- Mrs. Karadzic, "Just a second, please, the right time." You say, "Really."

utterances.speaker: MRS. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Yes, and just a moment. But just let me finish. You should just finish about what Cengic said." And you say, "Well, no, Cengic said, and he didn't feel right about not being in the negotiating team. He says he said to Alija, 'Why are you putting a man of conflicts there when he managed to cause an argument between me and the Muslims rather than the Serbs and the Muslims?'" What is that about, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, there were negotiating teams of the three parties. Mr. Cengic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think I know what the problem is, Your Honour, it won't occur again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, go on, please, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Please do.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three sides had their negotiating teams and these were all set up by the head of the teams, Karadzic, Kljuic, and Izetbegovic. And now here, Mr. Cengic, and this is Muhamed Cengic, I assume, yes, it is, he was the vice-president of the SDA, and he had high repute in the party. And Mr. Izetbegovic, the late Izetbegovic, didn't put him on the team as a member. Now, it was considered a great honour and then there was a little rivalry between the members of the team, and those who weren't on the team, so as far as I know, this was an individual who was characterised by Mr. Cengic as being one prone to conflict, and he says he managed to cause a rift between us and the Muslims. I think this is related to Mr. Mahmutcehajic and it refers to him. And Mr. Cengic says this because there is a certain amount of jealousy there because he wasn't on the team himself. And a little fact, too: Because that's how things were, and he says, well, he had fairly good relations other wise with the Serb side. Mr. Cengic did, I mean, that he thought he would be more useful on the team rather than the person appointed by Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic arrives home. He then takes over the conversation with you and very soon he says, "This is not assembly business. This was more party business." What does he mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm joking a bit here, why no one knew where he was. So I sort of criticised him for that. Whereas he's presenting a fact and he says that it wasn't assembly business but party business, because in our party you had a differentiation between party business and the rest, and Mr. Karadzic, as I said, met with the president of the HDZ at the time, Mr. Boban, and so - how shall I put this? - he identifies this because you always strove -- well, he even referred to it in psychiatric terms and said that we were on -- like on a football team. There is the management board and those who know the business best work in the state organs just like football players playing on a team. So that's why he says this was not assembly business. It was more party business.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Turn if we may to the last intercept of this bundle. It's one between you and Mr. Karadzic on the 2nd of March of 1992. It needs a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like this one to be played and the Prosecution have kindly agreed to oblige in that regard. But again, if it goes wrong, it's my responsibility not theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please play the transcript -- the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "I'll come within half an hour to the corps command." "It's live telephone connection into the programme. Wait a moment. Hello, uncle Momo, please wait just a little. He's still talking." M: Oh, really? XW: JuTel. M: Excuse me. XW: I'm talking to them mere. Just a moment. R. Yes. M: What's up? R: Were you watching JuTel? You weren't? M: No I wasn't. R: Well, I was talking directly to Izetbegovic. That started a secret mobilisation. M: A secret mobilisation? R: At all points, they are attacking everywhere. M: How? R: Well, they are attacking our settlements in an organised fashion and so on. M: Did you say that? They are attacking Pale? R: Excuse me? M: Did you say that they are attacking Pale? R: Well, yes. I received the information from up there. They are -- there are wounded, they can't get through. M: Really? R: Yes, yes. M: Where is that? R: Just a moment, Momo. Toso Domazet [phoen]. On JuTel, right, the police are distributing weapons to Muslims, of course. Of course. Well, I'm going to the corps headquarters now and we'll see what. Thank you very much. All the best. M: Hold on. You have that information. Maybe it's not -- there is a lot of misinformation. R: Look here. There is misinformation but we also have some pretty accurate information. There isn't a single Muslim settlement in which they haven't started. M: That's the thing. They are getting organised and putting up barricades but there is no place that -- I don't know. There is a lot of misinformation. R: There are wounded. There are wounded. M: There are wounded even in Zabrdje but that's not true, you know. It's only people talking, you know. R: Yes. M: Spreading misinformation. R: No, no. I'm getting information from people. There are people with gut wounds, leg wounds and -- M: You know. R: Excuse me? M: Where did you get that from? R: From Pale. M: From Pale? R: They are calling from Pale. M: And where is -- do you know, is anything going on in the city? R: Well, they are attacking in the city. That is approaching Vojkovici and these Grlica and Vojkovici settlements, they kidnapped a director of, what's it called, Famos and so on. I'm going to the corps headquarters with Kukanjac and Izetbegovic now. M: Yes, good. R: Oh, we received that memo from Cutileiro. M: Yes. What does it say? R: In which he says that the talks will continue on the 7th and 8th in Brussels. M: On the 7th and 8th in Brussels? R: Yes. Talks about geography and competences. There is no going back. M: Oh, please call and tell me what happened there. R: All right. M: I'll be home. But now down there in Reljevo, you know. R: All right. M: In about half an hour. R: All right. Bye. M: Bye."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What is going on in the intercept that we've just heard, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a very chaotic, confused conversation, and it would be really useful to understand it, to get to the bottom of it. First of all, Mr. Karadzic was on the phone with JuTel, and that was a television station for Yugoslavia. It created for itself the image of an independent station, although they weren't, really. There was a crisis going on. A member of a wedding party was killed in Bascarsija in Sarajevo. I think the father of the bride was killed. And now Mr. Karadzic and -- Mr. Karadzic and.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the name of the other person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were talking through JuTel about the possibility of going to see Mr. -- sorry, General Kukanjac in the corps headquarters, to try to see whether the army can restore some order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the second name you mentioned. You said and now Mr. Karadzic and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karadzic was talking to late Mr. Izetbegovic through JuTel. That was the beginning of that conversation. And they had agreed to go to the second military district to see Kukanjac. And then continues the conversation between Mr. Karadzic and me, in which he informs me about what he knows about attacks on Serb areas, the number of the wounded and so on. And at one point I tell him there is a lot of misinformation circulating. We need to distinguish between what is true and what isn't. And I quote to him the example of my village, Zabrdje, because the current information circulating is that there are people wounded there, and I tell him I know that there aren't any. And he tells me, all right, but there are conflicts in other places, clashes and skirmishes. The overall atmosphere is one of mistrust and disinformation being deliberately put out to mislead the other side. That's the focus of our conversation and I am asking him to pass on the information that he gets when he goes to the 2nd Military District because I am also very concerned. There were some barricades put up at that time and there were some conflicts, but nothing was so dramatic as it seemed at this point. It was mostly fear that was feeding the frenzy. And at one point, Mr. Karadzic told me that he had heard Serbs were attacking Sarajevo as we talked, which was wrong. Disinformation was circulating in abundance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For those of us who were only able to listen to this intercept in translation, how would you assess the tone of Mr. Karadzic's voice as he was speaking to you on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how the people who listened in to this conversation managed to transcribe it. It must have been very difficult. It's not exactly authentic. There are many interjections. Mr. Karadzic was anxious and panic-stricken because he was afraid that war had broken out. He had heard a lot of bad news. I suppose, and I heard later, from JuTel television, that Mr. Izetbegovic was also saying to him, "Your men are coming on from Pale." That was in the conversation they had through JuTel. It was played on TV the other day, and I even saw that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've now got a few minutes of questions about the shooting at the wedding and the barricades that Mr. Krajisnik has just referred to. I'm in the Court's hands as to whether to deal with that now or immediately after the break. Mr. Stewart will then take over after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could do it within the next seven minutes I'd like you to do it now. If not, then we'll have a break first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the shooting at the wedding that this Chamber has heard a fair bit about, and you have just mentioned. When you receive news of this shooting, what was your reaction, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Josse and I watched footage of an interview during the proofing. It is not authentic. It's done by a journalist from Great Britain. We were in the delegation, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Buha and myself, attending a meeting somewhere abroad. Geneva or Brussels. And that day, we had arrived in Belgrade because we always took the plane from Belgrade, either to Geneva or to Brussels, and in Belgrade we got a report that somebody was killed at his son's wedding. He was killed by a member of the Patriotic League, a man who is on trial as we speak. The Prosecutor in Sarajevo, a Serb, qualified this as not an ethnic incident but as a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Go on. But a little slower please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. This entire activity in Sarajevo is being led by people who are in Sarajevo, Mr. Dukic and Mrs. Plavsic, and there are discussions in the Presidency because both sides had put up barricades, first Serbs and then Muslims. And then it had to be dealt with, various demands were put forward. So we had a conversation with them from Belgrade. When I say "we," I mean Mr. Karadzic spoke on our behalf trying to get as much information as possible. And what was wrong in that interview is this: When I say "we," I use this word "we" all the time but I didn't actually invite anybody to participate with me because we were unable to do anything at a distance, any way. I have a couple of things to say about that interview but I'll wait until we get to it. For both the Serb and the Muslim side, and I'm talking about politics now, it was a very unfavourable incident. It was certainly done by an individual who was a greater Muslim than late Alija Izetbegovic, and maybe his group of extremists, but to us, it was a terrible shock because nothing like that had ever happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina, such disrespect for national emblems, whether it was a Serb or a Muslim, with their flags, it was unheard of that the person would be killed and his flag seized. That killing of a Serb at a wedding was the first situation that could have served as a spark for the war. Thank God for those people who were there then, Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Ejub Ganic, who was head of the Crisis Staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there were Mrs. Plavsic and they -- and Mr. Dukic, and they dealt with the situation. But it is still believed that this was a fatal incident that contributed to the outbreak of the war, although the war actually broke out a month later, not then. Why do I say that the Muslim side actually, in my opinion, didn't want this? I read the memoirs of late Mr. Izetbegovic, and I read there that he was very unhappy over the incident because the referendum was about to take place, and it wasn't in his interest to give any food to Serb arguments. It was a very grave incident that could have had very grave consequences for a much broader area than Sarajevo, and later indeed it did have fatal consequences. So I maintain that it was bad for the Muslim side as well, although I have no reason to defend either the Muslims or Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The interview that you have just referred to, is the one that I handed you on Friday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For the Court that is P853, and as Mr. Krajisnik has said, perhaps we'll refer to it -- return to it later. Just want to ask you about the barricades, Mr. Krajisnik. It's said that these were erected by both sides spontaneously. What did you, the Bosnian Serb leadership, do about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just explain why I said it was spontaneous. The immediate reason was this killing. Nobody could have planned, logically speaking, that something like this would happen, especially not on the Serb side. So it -- if it did happen, it had to be spontaneous. I later made inquiries. It was certainly spontaneous on the Serb side. And why do you think it was spontaneous on the Muslim side as well? Because it was a reaction to this action they had taken. Excuse me, your question was what did we do. What we did was to deal with the whole situation a bit later. It took some time. An agreement was reached, a joint statement was drafted between Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Dukic on one side and Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Ganic on the other side. It was made as a press release and the situation was dealt with. And on the issue of barricades, Mr. Kukanjac came to the assembly to see me one day, I was very surprised, and he said, "Come with me, I'm going to Zabrdje, your home place." And we -- there were barricades on the way. We talked both to Muslims and to Serbs, asking them, Why are you doing this? And each side answered, We are afraid of the other side. Suddenly, there were weapons all around, and suddenly you see this great turnaround away from peace and you see yourself sliding towards war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could take the break now. I'd like to discuss with Mr. Stewart whether I should ask any more questions in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue the lifting of confidentiality of exhibits 152 up til and including 156, you'll find that on the 28th of February 2005, and where I may not have been -- it was in private session and where it has not been sufficiently clear where I said the confidentiality -- finally the confidentiality will be lifted, that of course should be understood as an order for the Registry to lift that but, of course, that takes some administrative activity before it really is lifted. I also draw the attention of the parties that although that has -- confidentiality has been lifted, that's true for the transcript, and it's true for the exhibits, but it's not true for everything related to that. That's clearly explained on these pages, the pages are 9544 and/or 9545. I have two different versions. Page numbering is not exactly the same. Mr. Stewart? Is it you or will we have some additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. We decided that Mr. Josse has concluded that bit for the moment though we may return in due course to one or two of those topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when we got to the end of the session on Friday, chronologically we had come up to the ends of February 1992 and we had just been considering some aspects of March. When we get to the beginning of March 1992 -- first of all very briefly, your -- your personal circumstances involved the continuing serious illness of your wife, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had the bad fortune that my wife was very seriously ill. She even spent some time in a coma.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was, just in summary, your day-to-day working life at that time? You were still living in Sarajevo. What was the length of your working day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have answered that question one of the previous times but I'm going to add to my previous answer. I am the kind of man who likes to work, and I work long hours. I worked long hours in my office, and I called home very often to keep in touch, to see how my wife was doing. Just as an example she was in a very bad condition at one stage and she had a fit. I got into a car with Abdulah Konjicija and we drove her to a hospital and hospitalised her and it was only thanks to that quick intervention that she pulled through. It was a heavy burden on me, I must say. As for work, March was the busiest month, because we had inter-party talks, visits by Mr. Cutileiro, travel, and although there were some assembly sessions, sessions of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina, most of my time was taken up by negotiations, either in Sarajevo or at international conferences in Geneva, Brussels, et cetera. So I had very little spare time, and would only have some time to spend at home on weekends. Otherwise, I came home very late at night. If you want more details, I can provide them. You can see even from the documents that it was a very, very busy month, filled with various activities, and all those activities were geared at finding a solution for the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. Krajisnik, you've said that -- the way you put it was, most of your time was taken up by negotiations. And you're talking specifically about international negotiations, are you, or when you referred to Sarajevo are you including domestic negotiations with other parties in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A constantly burning issue was what was going to become of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and talks were held at various levels, with president of the club, with some intellectual, with the party leader. Even within families, all discussions were about what kind of solution would be found for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Even at parties, people discussed the same issue. At the assembly we had the Presidency of the assembly, the president, vice-president, secretary, council chairman, and we discussed it all the time, trying to find a solution, and whenever there was a -- the smallest indication of a -- something positive, we were all very happy. The crisis developed very fast, as a cancer, and everybody was anxious to find a solution. I don't think there was any topic that was more important, even football was pushed on a back burner. Television was watched very closely, and every smallest development was weighed from the standpoint of whether it was good or bad for that issue. I always said that we should do our best to hold our assembly sessions, to keep the talks going, because as long as we keep up the contacts we are avoiding war. And when the war broke out, I must say, I felt --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction of the interpreter: Looking back I feel some remorse now over the fact that I spent so little time with my family, but the situation was such that I simply couldn't help it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, so far as the continuing European Community and Cutileiro talks were concerned, is this correct, Mr. Krajisnik, that as well as meetings with Mr. Cutileiro and his colleagues, you were having -- in March 1992 and possibly towards the end of February, you were having separate discussions with representatives of the Croat community? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were those -- the fact that you were having those discussions, was that known to Mr. Cutileiro?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In hindsight, I'm afraid of making a mistake now, but one thing is certain: Mr. Cutileiro was a wonderful man, a brilliant diplomat, who always encouraged our bilateral talks. He wanted us to sit down together, bilaterally or in a tripartite setting, if bilaterally then not to the prejudice of the third side, to keep talking and trying to find a solution. There was one meeting when he knew that we went from Brussels to Graz to meet with the other side. Any side could meet with another side, but there was no solution without involving the third side. Cutileiro encouraged it all. He said, "Do whatever, just find a solution. The European Community would be only too happy."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did the negotiators for the Bosnian Serbs continue to be you, Dr. Karadzic, and Mr. Koljevic? Did they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mainly the three of us, although there were other people involved. The other people were mainly experts. The three of us were the main negotiators. I can even say why it was the three of us, if you think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I won't ask you about that now, Mr. Krajisnik. If you -- if you can put some sort of figure on it, over the whole of the month of March 1992, roughly what proportion of your total working time was devoted to the international negotiations? And I include the meetings, any preparation, any work related to those.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hardest thing for me to answer is when you from the West ask me for a number. Whatever number I give you, it won't be accurate. I keep telling you we worked on it all the time, both at the office and amongst us, and so on and so forth. Those international talks are a matter of common knowledge. You can find about it from newspaper reports, in Sarajevo, in Brussels, in Lisbon, in Geneva, but apart from that, contacts took place on a daily basis. Maybe not literally on a daily basis but we worked continuously and constantly tried to tie up the loose ends that were sometimes minor or looked minor but they were important to the overall solution. Unless you tell me that I didn't answer your question, I will tell you that we were happy when a mediator appeared. And our domestic meetings in Sarajevo served as a preparation for international talks. We wanted to clear up some issues that needed sorting out before we came to Geneva or wherever. One witness here talked about all the places we've been, the only place we haven't been is the US, it seems. All the work we were doing was aimed at resolving the crisis and I cannot give you a number because it would be sheer guesswork, two times or five times, 10 per cent or 15 per cent, it would all be speculation, but our main concern, our main job, all our -- all of our work was geared at solving the crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, Mr. Krajisnik offered to explain to us why it was the three of them that were the negotiators and I'd like to hear that explanation, since it's not in every jurisdiction that the assembly speaker would participate in foreign negotiations. Therefore, I'd like to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you please give that explanation, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart was talking about, or rather asked which three talked to the other side, I mean the Muslim and Croatian side. Of course, later on, as a delegation of the Serb side in the negotiations. Mr. Karadzic had close relations with the Croatian side, if I can put it that way, and the Croatian side was well disposed towards Karadzic. The Muslim side several times expressed the desire to have Krajisnik on the team and then they criticised me, the Serb side criticised me, saying that the Muslim side had liked me, in a way. And they would say, "Well, I like it when Krajisnik comes in to express some views." What I mean to say is -- well, it did have some depth to it but what I want to say is that it was difficult, once you're in a conflict, sometimes the delegation is decided on by the other side. We didn't meddle into the affairs of the Croatian side or Bosnian side in setting a delegation but Mr. Koljevic and I myself, who were in the Bosnia-Herzegovina delegation, we stayed in that delegation but what I said a moment ago helped a little. And that's why I said, I gave you the example that Mr. Karadzic was on a secret visit to the -- went to the Croatian side on a secret visit. Sometimes one side prefers talking to one person rather than another person. Well, that might not be too important but it is nevertheless a characteristic or a secret of negotiations and just a fact of life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I must admit that I was a bit confused because I didn't follow the question because the question was about negotiators for the Bosnian Serbs, where I still in my mind was with the international negotiations, where the question clearly pointed at the domestic negotiations between the parties. But even that confusion now has been taken away. So thank you. Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to add something to that question. Was there a type of -- or let me rephrase my question. Who made the decision that those three people would be the negotiators, you being one of them? Was there a meeting, for instance, an SDS meeting? Were there deputies of the assembly who decided on this? Was there a mandate? And who gave you this mandate? Please tell us, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll answer straight away. The meeting of the 24th of October, and later meetings, too, put forward a certain number of people who would be in a position to negotiate with the opposite side. As far as I know, there were five or six of them, Karadzic, Koljevic, Krajisnik, Plavsic, Maksimovic, and Buha. And on the 27th of July, and you'll find that in the assembly, after the 12th of May, the first assembly during the war, the question of who would be a member of the delegation arose and we were supposed to go to London, and as we had a deputies club, I saw that many people wanted to be members of that delegation. I offered not to go and I asked for somebody to replace me, and you'll be able to read that in that assembly session. And there was a lengthy discussion and the upshot of it was, we authorised those six individuals or rather Karadzic can say who the three best men would be, and Karadzic explained this. He said the Muslim side likes to see a tete-a-tete meeting but I would like to have more people present so that it is not a tete-a-tete negotiation, because that would be like some sort of complicity. There was a second meeting where -- which was in Bijeljina. I saw that certain people were jealous of me. Not Bijeljina, Zvornik. I apologise, it was Zvornik. So to have me part of the delegation was something that the assembly had decided and that Mr. Karadzic had decided for the international negotiations. And you can see all this on the basis of the assembly meetings and the stenograms of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the experts that you referred to, that was at page 36, about line 9, as being involved, you're talking there about technical experts rather than people drawn from the deputies or other politicians that we've heard mentioned, are you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're quite right. They were foremost lawyers. First and foremost, people well-versed in the law who were necessary for negotiations of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, during the month of March 1992, we know it's a matter of record, there were five assembly sessions, though two of them were held on the same day, the 24th of March, one straight after the other, there were sessions on the 11th, the 18th, two on the 24th and one on the 27th. So you've told Their Honours about your work in relation to negotiations and there were those assembly sessions. Did you have any other areas of practical responsibility during that month?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember anything special, anything of particular importance, but I'm not sure what you would like to hear. I was very busy going about my assembly business and taking part in the negotiations. I had my hands full. And I didn't take part in any party business. Those assertions are just not correct. I didn't have time to do so and for purposes of illustration, all the Executive Board meetings for example of the SDS I was not able to attend a single one, whereas Karadzic, Koljevic, and others did attend. I could have attended in the capacity of guest but I just didn't have the time to do so. It took up too much of my time, and in addition to the private problem that I had, I tried to whittle my business down to what I had to do and you can all see all this on the basis of the documents available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you have, during that month, contacts with representatives of municipalities at which you discussed any issues of organisation within the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my responses to your questions I said where I was during my one-year term of office. I don't remember whether anything similar happened in March but I did not take part in discussing how a municipality would be organised, for instance. Perhaps there might have been a problem once or twice, and there should have been a mediatory role. For example the Novo Sarajevo municipality, in the case of that municipality, that was presented here was something that I helped overcome. If a delegation would come and visit me and I'll quote an example, I don't know whether it was March or not, but anyway a delegation from Drvar came to see me or rather came to see Mr. Karadzic and he said, This isn't party business. Go and see the president of the assembly. When they came to see me, my wife was in a very serious situation at the time. They were arguing in Drvar, which is only inhabited by the Serbs, about how some construction work was going to proceed, who would get what land and so on. I tried to solve this problem because unfortunately at that time the Serbian municipalities went to Muslim -- to Serb representatives, the Muslims went to the Muslim and the Croats went to the Croatians and as a Serb municipality, they came to see me, although it wasn't within my remit at all. And I just finished all that business and went to visits my wife and I happened to return and they had managed to argue amongst themselves again, and a delegation went on location to visits the site, to see what was going on or maybe I went myself, to see what I could do, but you have the constitution and the rules of procedure for the assembly, the assembly of Republika Srpska did not, pursuant to the constitution, have any authority over the municipal assembly, and by the same token, neither did the president of the republican assembly, he had no jurisdiction over the municipal assemblies. All he could do was to be the mediator or to assist in solving a problem but he couldn't do anything, he couldn't replace anyone or anything like that. You can see the rules of procedure governing the assembly and you'll be able to find that in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I suspect you're probably going a little fast for -- faster than is comfortable for all concerned, so I'd suggest that perhaps you go a little bit more slowly. Did you in the month of March 1992, have any meetings with representatives of any Crisis Staff of any municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having had any such meeting. As for the Crisis Staffs -- or, rather, with the Trial Chamber's permission, I would like to give a brief explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, I think you're perfectly entitled to give any explanation which is part of an answer to the question, of course.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff, as a title, in our former system, was a customary body which was established and which is established when a crisis breaks out and that's why it's called Crisis Staff. If there was a strike in a company or if there was a flood or anything like that. So that was quite normal. I don't know whether this has been written down anywhere, but it was normal to set up a body with that name. People would get together and this ad hoc body would step in to solve a problem. That's why I'm trying to be very precise here, because I don't think it's a lack of understanding but reference is made to Crisis Staffs which had a political role to play. Apart from the Novo Sarajevo, if you remember that discussion, where the two parts were -- sides were in conflict, I didn't understand this to be any Crisis Staff, but that it was a dispute between the party and people who were in authority. And I know that a man came to see me and another man went to see Karadzic, and then we brought the two together and discussed the matter, discussed the issue. So I'm quite sure that I did not talk to any, in inverted commas, Crisis Staff. I don't excludes the possibility that it was indeed a Crisis Staff but I wasn't conscious of it being a body with that name as a separate body. A Prosecution witness from Doboj explained all this on one occasion, when he said, well we had Crisis Staffs, too, and was quite normal to form Crisis Staffs in situations of crisis. Especially with war looming. Anybody could set up a Crisis Staff. And there is a piece of information from Bratunac. In June 1991, for instance, a small village set up its Crisis Staff and nobody knew about it. So that's my answer, my attempt to explain the situation to you as it existed. We didn't consider this to be anything bad. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, you referred when Mr. Josse was asking questions earlier to the incident about the killing of somebody involved in a Serb wedding. Whatever precisely occurred on that occasion, there seems to be general agreement that it was the 1st of March 1992. Just going ahead for the moment to early -- late March, early April, within that range, what did you regard as the start of the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I criticised the reporter who reported erroneously, and asked for your assistance in the matter, was interpreted in the following way: That a referendum which I blamed the SDA party for, was the main cause of the war. I did not say that. Nor was the referendum the main problem. The Serb people called for a plebiscite and war did not break out. I consider and I still do consider today, that it was the premature recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, without any transformation, as was promised, was one of the triggers for creating this unhealthy mood, and we can blame anyone we like for that. If you look at the consequences you don't know who began it all, who started it all, but I cannot, and I'm sure that Mr. Stewart will allow me to explain. At that time, the Muslim side was faced with a great problem. The European Community said, have a referendum, we'll recognise you and you'll get a state. It's no secret the Muslims in ten years' time, with their birthrate, could have had a demographic majority. Now to Momcilo Krajisnik, the European Community in 1993, and I was a member of the delegation with Mr. Buha, said something similar, and offered a similar, attractive conclusion, and we signed a declaration in September 1993 in Geneva where we said, We'll have Bosnia-Herzegovina for five years and after that Republika Srpska can vote to step down from Bosnia-Herzegovina and just as I signed as Messrs. Stoltenberg, Owen, and Izetbegovic signed as well, Mr. Izetbegovic was prone to take this up, was tempted to do so. But I think that the blame should be placed on the speedy recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was clear that the Serbs were against because this was done unconstitutionally and that, as far as I'm concerned, was the main reason for the war breaking out. And the mobilisation and everything else that followed, all that was an act that was not well thought out. And once war broke out, it was difficult to retain anything, so as far as I was concerned, the referendum, and Their Honours saw this, we held a meeting, we said we have nothing against a referendum at all. We are going to consider that it is a voice for the peoples to declare themselves and express their wishes but the mediators are there to decide, to act as arbiter and to say that such and such a thing should be done. Now, what caused disquiet among the Serbs was the fact that the convention on national minorities was asked to be accepted, adopted. If you were a nation to begin with and then were supposed to turn into a national minority this led to a great deal of disquiet. I'm quite certain that that war was not caused or started by the Serb people. It was politics. Now, on a local level, there were of course various incidents that broke out. So this was an explanation that I wanted to give. And thank you, Your Honours, for giving me the opportunity of giving that explanation. Now, the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina knows this and each and every man knows that. People living over there know what I'm talking about. You can't hide anything. And it would be unjust if I said, Yes, there was a referendum and you yesterday, the Serbs, went ahead with a plebiscite, there were no incidents, the Muslims were not against, so why would you be against it, without this -- against there unrecognised referendum? But what happened was the premature, speedy recognition, and that's what led to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, then, the question now I'm putting to you relates to, not then the causes of the war, but when it started. And just to remind ourselves, the referendum that you've referred to was held on the 29th of February and the 1st of March. The wedding incident that has been considered today was also on the 1st of March. On all the evidence we've heard in this case, it's perfectly clear that by the second half of April, a war had broken out. In that range, though, Mr. Krajisnik, at what point did you say to yourself, "We are at war. We haven't avoided war, there is war"? At what point did you consider that was the position?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for asking me that. Your Honours, you see, a month went by, at least a month, from the referendum up until the war, 4th or 5th of April, and that's when recognition came about. Throughout that time, from the referendum onwards, we held negotiations and sought solutions. Had that not been the case there would have been war at the beginning of March. So the essence of it was this: When the other side learned that Bosnia would be recognised, mobilisation was called, and this was proclaimed by the Presidency, unconstitutionally, the rump Presidency, without the Serb representatives, and that mobilisation was the spark. It was like bringing a lighter to some petrol. If you engage in mobilisation without Serb representatives, it wasn't the result of a foreign enemy, it was aimed against the Serbs, that the Muslim and Croatian representatives had proclaimed a mobilisation, and Mr. Stewart knows this full well.
