He's going to ask me what I did to have Izetbegovic withdraw the decision, which I thought was a very dangerous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: During the month of March, then, and that early part of April, so we've got a period of about five weeks from the referendum up to the date which you identify as essentially when the war started, were, first of all, you personally involved in any preparations by the Bosnian Serb SDS leadership for an imminent conflict?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not I personally, not only I personally, but nobody was included in that. And here is a piece of information in that regard. On the 5th or 6th of April, a so-called large-scale rally was organised of the assembly in front of the Holiday Inn. There might have been 50.000 people or 100.000 people attending. It was organised by the other side, whether the opposition or whoever. The leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party was in the Holiday Inn building itself and at one point, a television speaker said that from the Holiday Inn, which is a hotel nearby the assembly, that the snipers were targeting the people. And all these citizens went into the Holiday Inn and it was very difficult for Buha, Koljevic, Karadzic, the leadership, to escape and reach Serb territory, if I can put it that way. Had there been any preparation, they would have been there -- they wouldn't have been there where they could have been captured. And later on, on television, they showed a young man who was the secretary in the Secretariat of Mr. Karadzic, as a sniper, and I just had to laugh because the man had nothing to do with any of it. He was just a clerk, a white collar worker in some administrative department. So quite certainly, there were no preparations whatsoever. Let me repeat this. We believed 100 per cent that the Yugoslav People's Army was fully capable of protecting our people and that we would be able to find a solution. The peace process was to topple Izetbegovic and the national party and they made a national -- formed a national assembly which did not wish to leave the assembly building and to call for new elections. They wanted either to kill or to capture Mr. Karadzic. That was their aim. And all this is contained in the articles that appeared at that time. You can check it out quite easily. And let me just add, as far as I personally am concerned, the day before I was in the assembly myself, sitting in my own offices, and I was supposed to go to work that morning. My escorts came by with the driver and said something is happening in front of the assembly, something is going on, and they said, "You stay where you are and we'll go to the assembly building to see what's going on. And if the situation is safe, we'll come back and get you." What happened was that my escort was taken prisoner and we had a hard time exchanging him. That's why I didn't go to the assembly that morning. So that's what I thought, that war could break out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: During that five-week period and from the beginning of March, after that wedding incident, did you observe, yourself, anything in Sarajevo by way of violent conflict or by way of a sign of likely imminent conflict?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already described to you, Mr. Stewart, one incident when Mr. Kukanjac came to my office to escort me to my own house, to my own home. I wondered why he had come to see me, but the reply became obvious very soon. I was the only one who lived on the periphery, outside of town. Everybody else lived within a circle of half a kilometre from the office. So he had come as a military man, to protect me by his own presence. On the way, we came across barricades, manned by various people. And everybody was seized by fear. Whenever an incident occurred of an ethnic nature, even if it was just about regular crime, it assumed new dimensions because it happened within -- sorry, between persons of different ethnicities. However, there is a lot of wishful thinking in people and you tend to minimise whatever is going on, especially since we were maintaining negotiations and we were receiving various favourable reports as well, and thanks to those reports, I maintained my faith in a good solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you see barricades yourself in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. For the sake of truth and God himself, I'll tell you something. I came across a Muslim barricade in a village next to my own, the village of Sokolje and I saw some people there who said, "Just don't attack us yourselves because we will never attack you." And I was happy. I came back to Zabrdje and I told people, "See what kind of message I got? On the local level you can achieve apparently much more than you can at a global level." You heard Zekerijah Smajic who gave that interview and his telephone conversation but believe me, when General Kukanjac and I talked to those people, they were holding weapons without knowing apparently what to do with them. It was just one time when I simply went along the road and I saw those scenes. I heard about other barricades, but that's not my firsthand experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This was a -- was this a barricade in the nature of a check-point that you had to pass through or something else?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We called that barricade, although it's actually a roadblock. There was an armed group of people who stood there and stopped passersby. That's the kind of, quote unquote, "barricade" that I saw on that occasion. There were roadblocks later as well. I talked to that group. There is a fountain nearby, we drank water from it together and talked. It was on the 4th of April, just a few days before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So during the period from the beginning of March to 4th or 5th of April, were there any active preparations for Serbs for an imminent conflict, of which you were personally aware?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered most sincerely that I didn't know about any preparations, and I'm certain that everything concerning the Holiday Inn and the leadership and all that I told you about. All the information I had told me that there would be no conflict, and then the fatal moment occurred. I had no information from the ground or anywhere else that a conflict was in preparation. All the elements that I had indicated that a solution would eventually be found. I know that Mr. Karadzic didn't even take his elementary personal effects with him that day. I'm not speaking in defence of Mr. Karadzic. I'm telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any sort of war planning group within the SDS leadership in March 1992, whatever its title or name?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard a lot of bragging at various assembly meetings about people arming themselves, but as far as I know there was no plan, at the republican level or otherwise, for war. But there was a lot of bragging. People liberating this town and that town, arming that group or that village. It was sickening. There was even a book that we saw here, "Who is who in Republika Srpska?" There is no Krajisnik there. There are a lot of braggarts there featuring in that book. Everybody wanted to be in that book. War brings with it a lot of vice, and among other things bad things suddenly acquire a value and are praised and bragged about. I am certain that there was no plan. Why otherwise would they be in Holiday Inn that day? I really can't think of anything that could even remotely be used as evidence of the existence of such a plan that anybody could point out, because as I said, we were relying on the JNA to keep the peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I now want us to go back, please, to an exhibit. I wonder if you can be given Exhibit 412.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is minutes of ministerial council of the Assembly of the Serbian People, Sarajevo, 13th January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We've seen this document before, Mr. Krajisnik, not in the course of your own evidence. Do you see that it was chaired by Mr. Simovic and it lists a number of members of the ministerial council. The ministerial council was a newly established body, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it correct that the ministerial council was effectively the first government of the Serb republic until you formally and technically established a government a couple of months later?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a small correction. The ministerial council meant that, just like deputies were simultaneously in the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the ministers in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina constituted at the same time the ministerial council or their deputies. And that body was supposed to deal with affairs that couldn't efficiently be dealt with within the government because it wasn't working properly. It's not a government as elected by law. These -- this body was made up of ministers on the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the Serbian people, and they were an executive body of the assembly, and you could say that the way Mr. Stewart put it is correct, and they were supposed to function as a government does.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you were present, your shown as present at this meeting as is Dr. Karadzic. That's at about the fourth paragraph. I just want to ask you about one item at the moment, which is at the foot of page 2 of the English version. It's under the heading, "Conclusion 2." It would be about a couple of pages into the document. There is an underlined - should be underlined anyway - heading, execution of tasks resulting from the declaration of the promulgation of the Republic of the Serbian people. Do you see that heading, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it in more than one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's in the middle of page 2, I think it is. That's --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Realisation of tasks that follow from the promulgation of the Republic of the Serbian people, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, I'm looking at the second paragraph under that heading, then, it says, "It was concluded that the priorities springing from the declaration included the defining of ethnic territory, establishment of government organs in the territory, and the economic disempowerment of the current authorities in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this respect it was pointed out it was necessary to draw a clear line between the regulations in force which are not contrary to the federal regulations and those republican and municipal regulations which would not be enforced on the ground." So the priority of defining the ethnic territory, how was it planned at that point that that would proceed? Who would do it? And what would they do?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really grateful that you brought this up, although there is another document, minutes from the ministerial council, and I thought it was a different one. What I want to say is, talks had already been held and it was already clear what kind of model the future Bosnia-Herzegovina should follow. It was clear that it was necessary to establish in which areas a certain ethnic community had a majority population. Since Bosnia and Herzegovina had already applied for independence, for recognition, this was a political move but also an actual move aimed at pointing out areas in which Serbs had a majority, and the ministerial council was supposed to identify it in negotiations so that we have arguments when saying this map needs to be adjusted, there is a little more population here and a little less there. On the 10th of December, when an invitation was sent to Bosnia and Herzegovina to apply for recognition, you saw how we reacted at that session of the 21st December. Your Honours, on the 9th of January, Republika Srpska was indeed promulgated, proclaimed. However, in the decision that was suggested by the team, by the leadership of the assembly, it was conditional. The OTP has it because they took it from the office of Mrs. Plavsic. It was formulated in conditional terms, namely that the decision would become effective if Bosnia was recognised as an independent state. On the 17th of January, forgive me for a lengthy answer, on the 17th of January, Mr. Karadzic said publicly, regardless of this decision, "We are not asking for a division of Bosnia. What we want is transformation of Bosnia." This was followed by the decision of the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where we had a bitter struggle for three days to find the right solution, as to when to call a referendum. It was supposed to be on the 25th of January. However, it all fell through. The referendum took place without the consent of the Serb representatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, for practical reasons, the Chamber would like to have an early break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we were looking at the exhibit, P412, the document on -- from the 11th of January. If we turn on in that document to -- it's under, I think, this big, broad heading 2. Do you see some numbered points?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot find it. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We could probably find another one for you, Mr. Krajisnik. I suppose you've been handed the actual exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll find it, because I turned it all over. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm looking at, Mr. Krajisnik, is page 3 of your version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's also page 3 of the English and it's numbered paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It should be right in the middle of page 3 of your copy, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really sorry but I have to take some time to look for it. When I was gathering up my papers, I must have --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can hand up another copy and then we can perhaps find that one later. It's in the middle of a batch but there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Don't worry, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm sure we can track the original one down later. The --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry about creating this little problem. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. The document that you've got open in front of you now, Mr. Krajisnik, if you go to the third page, at the very top of the page and it's just about halfway up above the middle of page 3 in the English, it says, "On the basis of the presented information, the ministerial council reached the following conclusions." And do you see the number of conclusions following there? And if we go to number 4, do you see that? "The working group comprising Mico Stanisic," do you see that? Page 3, about halfway down.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. A working group comprising Mico Stanisic, Dr. Vitomir Zepinic, Nedeljko Naic, and Bozo Novakovic will deal with the issues regarding the organisation and scope of national security and will frame a concept about this. Mico Stanisic is responsible for the work of this group. Are you able to say, Mr. Krajisnik, more specifically, what was contemplated there? The reference to issues regarding the organisation and scope of national security.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that members of the ministerial council were supposed to make their respective proposals, each in their own remit, a proposal of measures, a draft, a plan, that would help us in the negotiations, to adequately represent what we were seeking. When we look at it just at first glance, it looks a bit mysterious. I don't know whether it was the intention of the authors, but the purpose of this was to cover each area in the republic, to make a contribution to the plan that we expected would be signed. That was the purpose of this plan of the ministerial council. Maybe it was given as background material to the working group, but I don't remember whether they actually made something out of it. I know what the ministerial council was supposed to do. Everyone was required to make a draft, a plan, in their own area of expertise, for the negotiations, for the future plan to be signed, such as future bills, laws, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I don't want to cut you off inappropriately. The general scheme, and the general planning arrangements here can probably be seen by the Trial Chamber reasonably clearly from the nature or the contents of the document. I'm focusing specifically on that point 4. If you don't know, Mr. Krajisnik, then please say you don't know. But it's specifically that point, I'm asking if you can say more specifically what was meant by the work to be done by the working group comprising Mr. Stanisic and others, regarding the organisation and scope of national security. Can you identify the issues regarding organisation and scope of national security which were in contemplation there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what the task facing the working group was, but I cannot interpret exactly what this means from this distance because I don't remember these conclusions. I'm just looking at them now and trying to interpret them. Nothing in particular, in fact. I know that they were required to help us achieve as good a position at the negotiations as we possibly could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'll move on, then, to a different document. You can put that on one side. Well, actually, you could find it in there as well. It's 415. If Mr. Krajisnik could be given P415. Now, we again we have seen this document before in the course of the case, but quite some time ago. Mr. Krajisnik, it's a minute of a meeting held in Banja Luka on the 11th of February 1992. Now, you are not among the people listed as having been at this meeting. Mr. Krajisnik, would you first of all just please cast your eye over this document so that you can see what it is, and the question for you is whether, at the time, in February 1992, you knew that this meeting was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know. I had this document in my hands on two occasions. It was a surprise to me that this meeting was held, but I wasn't aware of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say you had this document in your hands on two occasions, are you referring to occasions during this trial or earlier occasions some years ago?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant during the trial, although I said two occasions. I'm not sure about two, but at least once during the trial. Maybe during the testimony of Mr. Mandic, I had this -- these minutes in my hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I really doubt for the Trial Chamber's purposes whether they are worried about how many times you've will it in the course of this trial. So we can look, and Mr. Krajisnik you're quite right it came up in the context of Mr. Mandic's evidence. The -- under the heading, "Names, Mico Stanisic", do you see that? That's quite early in this document, there is a heading, "Mico Stanisic." Do you see that? You're not looking, Mr. Krajisnik so --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It says, "The ministerial council's position put forth at the last session is that the territory of SRBH which is under Serbian power, this power has to be felt. The Ministry of the Interior, or the MUP, as we often refer to it as, of Bosnia and Herzegovina, SRBH, is held by the Muslims and not by the Serbs as the general public is being led to believe because the SDA, Party of Democratic Action, has about 1.000 people on reserve in the Stari Grad police station out of whom only 30 or so are Serbs who almost do not even have uniforms unlike the others who are armed with the most modern weapons. Work should be done on the organisation of a Serbian MUP, starting with municipal and regional branches to the Serbian ministry itself. The Serbian staff in the MUP has to be the source of the replenishment and supply of Serbian MUP and the guarantee that the resources will be distributed proportionally across the board. A minimum number of unresolved requests have to be collected at this meeting and sent to minister Alija Delimustafic, and an appropriate deadline should be proposed for dealing with those requests." Mr. Krajisnik, were you aware that work was to be done on the organisation of a Serbian MUP at this time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of negotiations, under every option considered, it was envisaged that every constituent unit has its own MUP, that the police, in other words, belongs to the constituent unit. And among the options considered for this future Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the option that we would have three MUPs, the Croatian, Serbian, and Muslim. As for this organisation you're asking me about, there was no mention of any practical or actual organisation. Instead, whenever there was talk about forming a certain body, it was a mild form of pressure on the other side aimed at encouraging them to continue the negotiations, and this contribution of Mr. Stanisic is mostly true about the Stari Grad municipality, that disagreements, and disharmony in the MUP and all the false presentations made in the public that the MUP is united, that there were no problems, that was not true. The reserve forces were being divided. Serb staff was not hired. The problem of discrimination was constant, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if we look, there are various contributions from people present at the meeting, of course, but if we look at the conclusions, which are on page 4 of the English, and will be at page 6 of your copy, your version, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a list of 19 conclusions. And number 1, the Serbian advisory board is hereby established at the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP, consisting of the Serbian staff in leading positions across all lines of work in the SRBH MUP. Did you know, at this time or shortly after this meeting, that such an advisory board had been established?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of it. I was aware of something else, though. I knew that there were fierce objections against Mr. Zepinic who, ex officio, was supposed to be the person number 1 on the MUP, and this must be a reaction against him in anger because he had not seen to it that Serb staff was equally represented in the police, and was not able to perform their duties. I know, from other meetings, that everybody attacked Mr. Zepinic over this. However, I wasn't aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, well, if we go back to page 2 of the English, we see a contribution from Mr. Andrija Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's at the foot of page 2 of your version. And he is saying, among other things, third paragraph, he says, "I would also like to voice my complaints about the work of deputy minister Vitomir Zepinic. He signs letters of appointment for Muslims in Doboj but not for Serbs." So that was typical of the sort of complaints being made of him at that time, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if we go back to those conclusions, the second one, number 2, is the Serbian advisory board at the SRBH MUP shall be headed by deputy minister, Momcilo Mandic, who would also make sure the conclusions are acted upon and carried out. 3, the Serbian advisory board, the SRBH MUP is hereby ordered to carry out all the necessary preparations for the functioning of the Serbian MUP after the adoption of a constitution of the Serbian Republic of BH, and then there is a deadline of 14th February for proposals on systematisation of jobs and so on, and 5, not a single decision on the personnel policy in the SRBH MUP shall be carried out without the prior consent of deputy minister Momcilo Mandic. Mr. Krajisnik, what was the -- sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There is, for example, an order being given in conclusion 3 there, the Serbian advisory board is hereby ordered to--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Am I going to fast, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- what was this -- do you know, Mr. Krajisnik, what was this group or body that was giving an order? We see the list of individuals. We see minutes of the meeting. Do you know what it was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This body -- I'm convinced, in fact, these are in a certain way the leading people of the Serbs on the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina coming from various areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as far as I can see from this. So they met here, and adopted these conclusions. It's an unofficial body, informal body, such a body did not exist. They simply met spontaneously, each one of them was -- had been autonomous in their respective jobs in Nevesinje, Bijeljina, in Sarajevo, some of them certainly on the republican level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I'm not going to go to every one of these numbered conclusions, Mr. Krajisnik, but let's go to 12, which says, "Establish a commission which will put forth proposals for the emblem of the Serbian MUP as well as other insignia by 1st of March 1992, 16, work intensively on the training and arming of our employees in the police. And then 18 is to inform the ministerial council of the aforementioned conclusions. Mr. Krajisnik, are these conclusions and decisions of this group in its meeting here, were they consistent with the position and policies of the leadership of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely, this is not in line with what we wanted. Everything that I saw here is mainly accurate, but there was an incident before the last meeting that probably had an effect on what later happened with the MUP and this self-proclamation. But these conclusions here are a product of a certain sentiment among the Serbian personnel of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they are thinking forward. Once the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is proclaimed, once a certain option is validated, we will give in this way our contribution in the shaping of the new police force. I repeat: In every option, it was envisaged that the police force would be under each constituent unit. So they were just planning ahead. We did not think it was in our interest to divide the police force while the negotiations were going on, and that's why what happened at the last meeting in Brussels came to us as a surprise, when Mr. Mandic sent that dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So at this point, in February, that we are talking about, February 1992, this was not in line with what you wanted in what specific respects?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All our activities were supposed to serve as political pressure in order to achieve a political solution to the crisis, all of them. We didn't want to make a single active move that would lead to conflict, and even this here, all that they did, it's really a meeting initiated by them, but they only held it after suffering a very unfair situation and a very bad situation in the MUP for a long, long time, and in particular the inadequate service of Mr. Zepinic, with regard to the Serb personnel in the MUP. This is the main reason why they were doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, and by reference to specific conclusions set out here, if it helps, Mr. Krajisnik, was the -- was the problem or the difference between this group's position and what you, the leadership, wanted, was it a matter of timing of these proposals or were there some of the proposals which were not what you wanted regardless of timing?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of timing, we only wanted everyone to make certain proposals in their own area of expertise as a contingency plan for a certain political solution that was already a writing on the wall. We never intended to make any radical, unilateral moves. There are certain conclusions that might look like -- like it. They may look like a gauntlet being thrown, like something being done contrary to an agreement that hadn't been reached yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the SDS leadership want eventually to have a separate Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leadership of the Serbian people, or rather the negotiating team to be more precise, and the broader platform, in fact, was that we wanted what was proposed by the European Community, and that was that the constituent units -- that the MUP be within that constituent unit which would not be literally Serb but would be composed of a proportionate number of persons from that constituent unit. In the Republic of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the majority would be Serbs in the police force because the majority of the population would be Serb there. But we are talking about peace and about negotiations. So this Serb MUP was divided under abnormal conditions. There were cadres set aside in every municipality, not on the basis of a political settlement but as the result of a crisis. So the negotiations provided for the fact that the MUP be within a constituent unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was this proposal or these proposals that we've just seen in the document we have just been looking at, were they subsequently referred to any group of which you were a member?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember these proposals. I don't remember ever having seen them before. When I came here, I saw these minutes, and all the rest of it, but I don't remember that anybody presented me with that document or things of that kind. Especially as I knew that anything that anybody else did was within the frameworks of preparation and political pressure, not the realisation of something that could be implemented in practice. That is the absolute truth of it. It should have exerted, served to exert pressure. We had no other way. This was one of the ways in which we tried to arrive at a political solution. We couldn't outvote anyone. We couldn't resort to the use of force or anything of that kind. This was the only way we could bring pressure to bear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I would like you to be given now, Mr. Krajisnik, P420.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the document says that a --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, 415, Your Honour. 415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm still -- the one you're asking questions about, Mr. Krajisnik, it says that the agreement reached at this meeting should be presented to the ministerial council and the assembly of the Serbian Republic of BH, and after its certification an action should be launched. Do you have any recollection of it ever being sent, even if you would not have seen it at that time, to the assembly of the Serbian Republic of BH, since it so expressly mentions it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it was sent, it must have been at the meeting. That is the logic of it. But I really don't remember. And I state now on the assumption that somebody sent this out, I assure you that had I received this, I would consider -- have considered it to be political pressure, not realisation. But everything is contained in the minutes, whether a report of there kind existed or not. I personally don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I simply observe that the particular citation that Your Honour has just given from the document is actually something said by Mr. Slavko Drazkovic [phoen], as opposed to what is contained in the conclusions of the meeting? The conclusion in 18 which I read earlier informed inform the ministerial council of the aforementioned conclusions. So Your Honour, you see my point, Your Honour. Your Honour put it to him it says in the agreement reached in this meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I fully do agree with you that it's one of the participants who said this and it's not part of the conclusions of the meeting. That's perfectly right that you draw my attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I thought I should do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if you could be given 420, P420, and we have seen this document before in the course of Mr. Mandic's evidence. It's signed by him, dated or stamped the 31st of March 1992. And it's sent -- it appears -- to the minister, that's the Bosnia-Herzegovina minister, and that was Mr. Delimustafic. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, this was a telegram or dispatch from Mr. Mandic, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The minister at the time, the Minister of was Mr. Delimustafic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes you're quite right. I understand. Mr. Alija Delimustafic was indeed the Minister of MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it's addressed to -- well, the English is perhaps not as crystal clear as probably the Serbian is but the -- it says, I'll just read, SJB, Public Security Services and SDB, State Security Service administrations, to all, then to the head, CSB, security services centre, to all, to the chief SJB, to all, to the chief SUP, the SUP Secretariat of the Interior, Sarajevo. So it's been given very wide circulation. That's clear, at least on the face of it. And it says, "At its meeting held on 27th March 1992, the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina in accordance with the political orientation of the Serbian people and the Sarajevo agreement, promulgated the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In addition, the Assembly of the Serbian People passed a number of laws and other regulations necessary for the functioning of the Republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In that respect it passed a law on internal affairs which shall be uniformly applied on the territory of the Republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina as of 1st April 1992, and appointed Mico Stanisic, until now an adviser in the BH MUP, as minister, and we'll come to that assembly session, Mr. Krajisnik, but he was appointed the Minister of the Interior. We do see that. "This law, among other things, regulates a unified Public Security Service, regulates and organises the National Security Service within the framework of the rights and duties of the Republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, regulates the duties and powers of MUP employees, mutual relationships and cooperation between the organs of the Interior and the education, professional training, and specialist training of employees, in order to conduct internal affairs on the territory of the Republic of Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, based in Sarajevo, is setting up the following security services centres as territorial units." And then they are listed. Banja Luka, for the autonomous regions in which they are placed but I'll just list the places. Banja Luka, Trebinje, Doboj, Sarajevo, Guglijevik [phoen]. "Within the above-mentioned security services centres, in order to carry out specific tasks and duties within the competence of the organs of internal affairs, public security stations are set up for the territories of municipalities. On the day this law comes into force, the Security Services Centres and public security stations of SRBH MUP on the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina are abolished and cease to function and their authority, i.e. tasks and duties, within the competence of organs of internal affairs, are taken over by the above-mentioned organisational units of MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. All employees in service on this -- on the day this law comes into force in the administrations at seat of SRBH MUP, as well as employees of the abolished CSBs and SJBs who so wish will be taken over by MUP of the Republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina which will secure financial resources for normal work, salaries, joint consumption, material expenditures, et cetera. Prior to the engagement employees are obliged to swear an oath of allegiance before the minister or an official authorised by him. The contents of this dispatch should be made known to all the employees of the SRBH MUP in order to provide objective and timely information and to avoid incidents or disagreeable situations." Mr. Krajisnik, did this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it's only now that the French interpreters have finished their work. Perhaps you're confusing that if you speak softly, that it goes less quickly. Gerald Moore wrote the book, Am I Too Loud? That's not the issue. It's, am I too quick? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, did this document have the approval of the Bosnian Serb leadership, including yourself?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. We were at the meeting in Brussels, I believe it was, when, like a stroke of lightening, this dispatch reached us and Mr. Silajdzic presented it and said, "We are negotiating. Take a look at this telegram that's just arrived." And may I be allowed to add something and tell you what happened before that and why this came about in the first place. But anyway, all three of us or four of us who were there, we were absolutely taken aback when we received this telegram. It is quite unfounded, in all its points. Nobody could do anything like this. I could analyse it point by point and tell us all the mistakes, the mistakes for which -- and the reason for which nobody had the right to send out anything like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, before I invite you to do that, do you know, then -- I'll rephrase that. Did you know at the time, when you received this news, anything about how it had happened that this document had been produced?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what are, then, the main points on which, as you put it, nobody had the right to send out anything like this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave the Trial Chamber the draft constitution and constitution that was adopted on the 27th, and I think the last page of that constitution states that the constitution would be dovetailed and harmonised with the negotiations on Bosnia and Herzegovina. So that was one of the provisions. Secondly, the law on MUP was adopted. However, it cannot be put into practice until the constitution is realised. The constitution was proclaimed on the 27th of March, but it was neither published in the papers or anything else, or ultimately was the government set up, and an assistant minister, who was not in charge of the ministry do anything like this. In Sarajevo we had Mr. Djeric, he could have been consulted. He was in Sarajevo at the time. And he was also the Prime Minister-designate. And this goes much deeper. Secondly, you can't organise a MUP. You have to go to the assembly. You can't abolish anything with a mere telegram. Now, what I want to tell you is why this was compiled and produced in the first place, in my opinion. Prior to our departure for Brussels, at the assembly on the 27th of March, and this was on the 25th of March, there was a press conference that was held on the Muslim side, and I have it here, and the Muslim side stated loud and clear, "We, throughout the negotiations, tried to defer the issue, not to be proclaimed the culprits because we had the international community and the Croats and the Serbs against us. We did not agree to the agreement reached in Sarajevo." So they were buying time. That's what they said. Whereas we went to the negotiations to finalise the agreement. So there was a press conference that was held by the SDA party, and we went over there to negotiate and to discuss matters, whereas in the meantime, there was some division in the MUP and we decided upon the division of MUP, they decided on the division of MUP, because they considered that nothing functioned any more. An irresponsible act. But we did not reach any kind of agreement in Brussels. If you want to see the document on the press conference, I can tell you what Mr. Ifran Ajanovic said, their man who held the press conference, how the SDA party behaved, and as we are talking about the end of March, he said, "We called the opposition, we called on the opposition, and all patriots in Bosnia-Herzegovina to attend a meeting to stand up against the agreement." And that meeting was indeed organised. I mentioned it a moment ago, when they attacked the Holiday Inn, and when problems arose in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I don't know whether you finished with the document. Otherwise I would have one question to clarify one of the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I haven't, but by all means, Your Honour, I don't have any problem with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you say in your testimony that this law could not become effective before the constitution would have been finalised. Is there any clause, and I don't know whether this law we are talking about is in evidence, yes or no. If we have a text, does it say anything about when it enters into force, which is, well, very common for legislation to say, at the end, this law enters into force at such and such date or after this or that happened. Do we have any information about that? I'm looking both to Mr. Stewart, to you, Mr. Krajisnik, and also to Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I had thought that I would -- I did have it here the other day but, of course, as luck would it, I don't have it with me right now. I thought I would have a look over night and then can pick that up first thing in the morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, are you talking about the law on internal affairs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the law on which Mr. Krajisnik just testified that it could not -- could be implemented without -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have a scrolling version so I can't make specific reference looking at the words to Mr. Krajisnik's previous reference so I can only respond to the specific documents that I know are or are not in evidence. For what it's worth I think the law on internal affairs is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is as well but, Your Honour, it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't find, please look at it overnight and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We will probably get --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- inform the Chamber tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It will take more time if we deal with it now than if we sort it out over night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, can I seek clarification? Excuse me I'll just have to now scroll up this screen. You said a moment ago or a few moments ago, that -- yes, yes, it's page 71, Your Honours, it was line 10. The answer you gave, you said, so there -- or part of your answer, "So there was a press conference that was held by the SDA party and we went over there to negotiate and to discuss matters, whereas in the meantime, there was some division in the MUP and we decided upon the division of MUP, they decided on the division of MUP because they considered that nothing functioned anymore." Now, I heard that as a correction in the course of your answer, I heard it, Mr. Krajisnik. I don't know whether anybody else suggests I'm wrong, as a slip of the wrong when you said we decided upon the division of the MUP, they decided on the division of the MUP but perhaps you would clarify who you were saying had decided on the division of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said they, and I meant MUP. That is to say the representatives of MUP in Bosnia-Herzegovina, both the Serb, the Muslim and Croatian, that they reached some sort of agreement in our absence. And this continued later on, but I was referring to -- just a moment. This telegram, this dispatch, if that's what we are discussing now, quite obviously it was taken at their own initiative but at one point in time, whether then or later, all the MUP employees decided about dividing up MUP. Now, I can't pinpoint the exact time but both the Serb, the Muslim and the Croat, they had -- well, I wasn't there at that meeting. I attended another meeting when Mr. Zepinic was there, and I can explain that but that has nothing to do with this and this division of MUP that I'm talking about. And as to the press conference, I can show you the document on it, if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, just a moment ago, can we be absolutely clear, you -- when you -- you talked about an irresponsible act. You said they decided on the division of MUP because they considered that nothing functioned anymore, an irresponsible act. You're talking about an act in late March 1992, are you, or at some other time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the end of March and beginning of April, so that's the critical point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's when the press conference was held; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 25th of March was when the press conference was held, before our departure or perhaps the 26th, before our departure for Brussels when all three delegations went to Brussels to attend the conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in that answer, you said but the name doesn't appear to be on the transcript, you said, "I can tell you what Mr." -- and then we have a blank on the transcript -- "their man who held the press conference, how the SDA party behaved." I'm afraid I don't remember whether you gave a name at that point, Mr. Krajisnik, that hasn't appeared on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Irfan Ajanovic held a press conference. He was the vice-president of the assembly of Yugoslavia before that, and he was a deputy in the Bosnia-Herzegovina assembly, and he was a high-ranking person in the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you receive this news in Brussels, what was -- was Dr. Karadzic there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was his reaction?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for all of us, when I say us, to all three of us, it was a great blow because we were blamed there, and he felt very uncomfortable, because it was a very bad political blow in the negotiations, because something was done in concrete terms, which upset any agreement, and the Muslim side made use of that to blame us and say that we were undermining the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was your -- well, consternation does seem to be an apt word to summarise what you've already described to the Trial Chamber. Was your, the Bosnian Serb negotiators, was your consternation made apparent to the -- to all the others there in the meeting in Brussels?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Silajdzic came in bringing a telegram. We thought it was a false telegram to begin with. And then it was investigated and seen that it was not a false telegram, and then there were -- he hurled blame at us, look at what you're doing whiling we are negotiating. And this wiped out everything that was said at the press conference. So it had such a negative impact, you were in such a negative position when you received something like that, a telegram of that kind as coming from your side and your side had done something like that. So we received it at the conference itself, the meeting itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Mr. Cutileiro in the room at that point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm looking at the clock. I don't know whether if you would say I can finish in one or two minutes, the line of questioning, otherwise I would like to invite you to continue tomorrow because I have for two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm more than happy to -- the reference to that law, those Article 126 is P64A tab 598 in case that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact I found it meanwhile. And I also found the article on which the -- since you are raising the issue, it -- Article 130 reads, "The present law shall enter into effect eight days after its publication in the Official Gazette of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina," whereas Article 129 reads, "General acts on internal organisation of the ministry and the Public Security Services shall be enacted within 15 days from the day the present law has entered into effect." Ten minutes ago, I was -- I had forgotten about matters but looking it up it clarifies matters. Therefore, only two matters. The first one is, Mr. Stewart, I hope that you received the update, as the matters stand now, the updated version of the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It arrived this morning, I think, Your Honour, or very recently. I've had it by e-mail extremely recently, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're invited to make further updates, that is to take any further published exhibits from the judicial data base. I inquired into the matter. It takes even without legal training, but for someone who is just administrative support, it takes approximately two exhibits a minute. So therefore, 100 an hour approximately. So we do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We thought it could be done a bit quicker Your Honour, but there were 2700 of them. But, Your Honour, there's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the bulk is there at this moment. I think it's only a limited number that would be added. The pace since Mr. Treanor and Ms. Hanson disappeared for the time being, we don't have the similar bulk material.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no problem about that. The value of having those 2700 is obvious. Could I just ask a small point, Your Honour, is -- perhaps I'm just not thinking through this clearly enough but the -- all we need for that purpose is it -- for it to be plainly identified for us which of the items which have just been added to the JDB. As long as we know that we can do that exercise. If we don't know that then we really are hunting around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact that Mr. Registrar is informing the team and Mr. Registrar to the extent possible would you please include the Defence, perhaps also the Prosecution, if they were interested to learn about it, in what had been recently scanned and has become part of the judicial database.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Haider already knows how helpful we have found his work over the last few days, Your Honour, for which I offer our appreciation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then before adjourning, Mr. Krajisnik, and after having instructed you again not to speak with anyone about your testimony, I just wanted to let you know that although the focus may be in questioning, of course, is on what was part of your professional duties, the Chamber will understand what it takes from you to be taken back to moments where not professional duties but also more personal matters were very important for you. The Chamber is aware of that, that that's also part of your testimony. We will adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tomorrow afternoon, same courtroom, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same courtroom, tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of May, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
